html:
Edward Wilmot Blyden was a writer, teacher and diplomat in Liberia and Sierra Leone, and one of the founding thinkers of Pan-Africanism.

He was born in the Danish West Indies. Turned away from colleges in the United States because he was black, he sailed in 1850 to Liberia, the republic founded by black American settlers. There he became a professor, president of Liberia College, secretary of state and ambassador to Britain. He also worked as an official in Sierra Leone and Lagos.

Blyden argued that Africans had their own history, culture and "African personality", which they should be proud of rather than copy Europe. In his book Christianity, Islam and the Negro Race (1887) he praised Islam in West Africa as more respectful of African ways than European missions. He learned Arabic and pressed for African-run schools and churches.

His ideas inspired later Pan-Africanists such as Marcus Garvey and Kwame Nkrumah.
sum: Edward Wilmot Blyden was a writer, teacher and diplomat in Liberia and Sierra Leone, and one of the founding thinkers of Pan-Africanism.
